en: He seized and swung.
At the cartilage of the right shoulder blade,
Your formidable, unfortunate mother—
He struck her then.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Cried out weeping and fell doubled up.
When Köbösh drew back and struck,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Then fell straight upon her head.
When she cried “Oh!” from her mouth,
Your sister-in-law’s blood came in heaving gushes.
Losing consciousness, her eyes rolling,
A night of ruin fell upon her.
Her forehead bone was sloping;
She was destined to see this horror.
When the hero’s eyes had closed,
Your sister-in-law’s days were ill-starred.
The hair at her nape was grass;
When the hero’s eyes had closed,
Your poor, fierce sister-in-law
Had many calamities to bear.
When slave Köbösh struck her down,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Lay embracing the earth.
As he was about to take her apple-like head,
As he was about to cut your sister-in-law up for the great dogs,
Slave Shuutu, with a felt cap like a yurt covering,
Manas’s close companion,
Seized Köbösh:
“Köbösh, you are no khan, you are worthless!
If you truly are a khan,
How could you cut off a woman’s head?!”
Exceptionally mighty hero Shuutu
Now spoke in varied ways.
Your dear, fierce sister-in-law—
Preventing Khan Köbösh from striking her,
He rescued your sister-in-law.
Her tongue did not speak; she said no word.
Your sister-in-law had lost her speech.
Taking no rest day or night,
Your sister-in-law lost her looks.
Unable to find a way to move,
Your sister-in-law lost her strength.
Darkness deepened before her eyes,
A day of trouble fell upon her burdened head.
Her rib bones split apart,
Her blood poured from her side.
For a day and a night,
She lay unconscious.
At midmorning,
She came to her senses.
It had driven the poor woman from her wits:
They had cut in two
The very child she had been nursing.
When she raised herself and looked,
There was no bluff where she could hide,
There was no food she could swallow.
There was no support on which she could rely,
There was no place where your sister-in-law could take cover.
There was no forest into which she could flee.
To anyone she might take as shelter,
There was none who would not bear her ill will.
Unable to collect herself,
A day of hardship fell upon her.
Upon your precious sister-in-law’s head
Fell a night no human should witness.
“My leopard lord, do not die!” she said.
“Let this wretched soul not see sorrow!” she said.
“If God creates someone as a living soul,
To any woman after me,
God, do not give such horror!” she said.
“My dear long, thick braid,
When my blue-maned lord died,
My poor head fell to plunder like this.
Winding my silken hair six times,
Why did I not braid it?
His fine mustache flattened,
His soul setting out toward the world beyond,
When he was in such a terrible state,
As a sacrifice to the sultan,
Why did I not die!
The living find their beauty in the land,
A woman’s life is with her husband.
My precious lord, do not die!
Fainting like this,
Let me, bereaved one, be spared disgrace.”
The place where your blood-shedding Manas died,
The place where bereaved Kanykey suffered abuse.
Drops from Talas’s springs—
In many places it left a mark,
The whip of the six scoundrels.
They had found an evil stratagem;
By the scoundrel who came from behind,
As she sat without keeping watch,
Your mother had her breast slashed open.
When she tried to walk, her strength failed,
Black blood flowed from her shoulder blade.
Having suffered this abuse,
Your mother wept bitterly;
Your mother saw it as fate’s decree.
Without showing that she was a woman,
She did not utter a word against Allah.
When she saw the plundered property,
When your precious Manas had died,
The countless riches left by the generous one—
Abyke and Köbösh, two scoundrels,
Chyybyt and Kochkor, making four scoundrels,
Adybay and Kölbay, making six scoundrels—
The countless riches left by the generous one,
When they divided them by whip lengths,
When they plundered the wealth,
When the slaves wrought terrible havoc,
When they entered and trampled from above,
When they opened the treasury,
“If they take my treasury, let them!”
That blood-shedding hero’s great mosque,
Surrounded by a garden of plane trees—
If soaked in water for forty years,
Its edge would not fade in the slightest;
If left in water for eighty years,
It would not come apart and rot:
The great carpet with golden patterns
Was nowhere to be seen when she looked.
Let alone the carpet, not even a stump remained;
Where it had gone was unknown.
Khan Manas’s great mosque—
They had cut down and felled its plane trees.
The six scoundrels of evil intent
Made war upon the mosque,
Flooded it with water and brought it down,
Felled all its willows,
Toppled all its buildings.
They had plundered it utterly.
Kara-Üngkür, where the treasury stood—
Its cave was left empty.
The treasure and gold coins
The six scoundrels had plundered entirely.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Then, between two thoughts,
Had survived without dying.
“When she is broken and her days run out,
She will heed what I say,” he thought.
“When the shameless woman has no recourse,
Then she will marry me,” he thought.
Did she know that was why the six scoundrels acted so?
Your lion mother Kanykey—
Would she marry one of the six scoundrels!
“My golden treasury that I gathered—
Such is its worth; let me scatter it.
These were my precious one’s words:
When a woman’s husband dies,
Only her own kin are close, he said.
Now I shall flee toward my own kin!
Until I return again,
Until I see my dear people,
Dear Talas, farewell!
Kara-Buura, broad valley,
Jylgynduu and Keng-Kol, great valleys,
Farewell, together with my land!
Until I return again,
Until I see those dear faces,
Never full when asking for food,
Never giving up their greed,
If driven forth in darkness,
Prowling like leopards,
Never shrinking from death,
Never turning back from their appointed end—
My dear Kyrgyz, farewell!
Those huge dogs attacked my migrating camp in Keng-Kol.
A curse upon being a woman!
Dear Creator,
Parted from my blood-shedding hero,
Thus I depart, unable to take revenge!
Those huge slaves plundered my gold in Keng-Kol.
Once my own kin inflicted suffering,
I left unable to avenge my hurt upon the dogs.
The dear bird called the wild duck
Turns in flight toward the open plain.
How much abuse I have suffered
For the child who came from my womb!
The wretched bird called the kite
Swoops in flight toward the open plain.
With no kin standing around me,
I am perishing, O God,
For the child who came from my womb.”
Her rib bones split,
Your mother resolved to flee,
Tears pouring from her eyes.
Then, unable to wipe her tears,
Unable to draw back the water from her nose,
She crept along, taking awkward steps.
The black blood flowing from her side
Trickled down her soft leather boots.
Exhausted, she wept and cried aloud.
When your mother tried to walk,
Every bone ached terribly.
Worn out and weary, unable to walk,
Wanting to die yet unable to die,
Unable to give up this accursed life,
Unable to find and cross a mountain pass,
Your mother could not reach a known place.
Exhausted, with night falling upon her head,
Your mother could not leave Talas:
“At the spur where the mountain ends,
At the headland of the level mountain,
Upon the face of broad Ak-Chiy,
At this edge of Talas,
Stands Khan Manas’s little enclosure.
Let me go to that enclosure;
Around the lord with whom I clasped hands,
Let this wretched soul make a circuit.
He was a lion of mighty spiritual power;
Let me receive a sign from him.
If there is no sign from him,
Let me die in that very place!
My lord Khojosan, lend me your hand!
In this dreadful day, my lord, grant me a way!
Abuse has fallen upon this wretched soul.
At this moment, O God,
Grant this black-faced one a way!
Parted from my mighty lion,
Must I go toward my own kin?
My surging land of Talas,
My teeming Kyrgyz people—
O God, must I leave them here?
From the support upon which I relied,
O God, must I truly be parted,
From my renowned Kyrgyz people?
Beaten by wind, struck by the breeze—
Is there one as wretched as the wind?
Parted from her excellent one,
Fleeing at a trot, fleeing on foot,
Is there one as wretched as I?
Widowhood fallen upon her head,
Is there one who sobs as I do?!
Taking Bukhara as my refuge,
I set out walking from Talas.
Is there one who wanders as I do?
My dresses of many kinds,
When I pull them up, will not reach my neck.
Without leaving me to languish, my betrothed,
My blue-maned one, draw me into your embrace.
Having my palace wrecked by dogs,
I suffered plunder and disgrace.
Who followed twelve spiritual masters,
My mighty lord, take me with you!
Your white-marked horses on the hills,
Thoroughbreds and fleet steeds mingled,
All brothers and kinsmen hostile,
The son you leave behind still young—
Without casting my soul into torment,
Take me, my lord, take me with you!
Your white-marked horses in the mountains,
Great steeds and wheat mingled,
The one who would tend the people without leaving them forlorn—
The son you left behind is young.
